```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)         # row index (also used as column index for A, which is M x M)
    j: dim in [0, N)         # column index of B (M x N)
    k: dim in [0, M)         # reduction index; same extent as i

data:
    # Lower unit-triangular matrix A (stored as full MxM, but only entries with k >= i are used;
    # A[i, i] = 1, A[k, i] arbitrary for k > i, A[k, i] never read for k <= i).
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE = (i, k) -> i + k * M
        # Column-major layout with respect to (i, k):
        #   - for fixed k (a column), A[0..M-1, k] are contiguous.
        #   - This makes accesses of the form A[k, i] (column i, varying k) stride-1 in k.

    # Matrix B, overwritten in place, logically used as both input and output.
    # Conceptually, B on the right-hand side refers to its value at kernel entry.
    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i + j * M
        # Column-major layout with respect to (i, j):
        #   - for fixed j (a column), B[0..M-1, j] are contiguous.
        #   - This improves locality when repeatedly traversing B[k, j] along k for fixed j,
        #     and when updating entire columns.

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE
    M: size_t    # number of rows (and columns) of A, and rows of B
    N: size_t    # number of columns of B

    # Tunable blocking / SIMD parameters (chosen per target machine):
    TI: size_t   # tile size in i (e.g., 64)
    TJ: size_t   # tile size in j (e.g., 64)
    TK: size_t   # tile size in k (e.g., 64)
    VEC_K: size_t  # SIMD vector width along k (e.g., 8 for AVX2 single, 16 for AVX-512 single)


computation:
    # Triangular update:
    # For each row i and column j, accumulate contributions from rows k > i
    # using the strictly lower part of A (A[k, i]) and the original B[k, j].
    #
    # This matches the C kernel:
    #   for (i = 0; i < M; i++)
    #     for (j = 0; j < N; j++) {
    #       for (k = i+1; k < M; k++)
    #         B[i][j] += A[k][i] * B[k][j];
    #       B[i][j] = alpha * B[i][j];
    #     }
    #
    # with the understanding that B on the right-hand side is the value
    # at kernel entry (conceptual B_in).
    update:
        for i, j:
            B[i, j] = B[i, j] + sum(k in [i+1, M), A[k, i] * B[k, j])

    # Final scaling by alpha (matches "B[i][j] = alpha * B[i][j]" in the C code).
    scale:
        for i, j:
            B[i, j] = alpha * B[i, j]


optimization:
    # 1. Tile the (i, j) iteration space so a working set of B plus the
    #    corresponding panel of A fits into cache.
    #
    #    After blocking, the logical iteration space is over tiles:
    #      I: tile index over rows (blocks of size TI)
    #      J: tile index over columns (blocks of size TJ)
    #      i, j: intra-tile coordinates.
    block(j, J, TJ)      # tile columns of B
    block(i, I, TI)      # tile rows of A/B

    # 2. Make column tiles outermost, then row tiles:
    #      for J       # column tiles
    #        for I     # row tiles
    #          for i, j inside tile (I, J)
    #    This drives the computation column-panel by column-panel, which
    #    improves locality and exposes column-wise parallelism.
    hoist(J)
    hoist(I)

    # 3. Within each (I, J) tile, reorganize the triangular update into a
    #    k-outer formulation to reuse A and B more effectively.
    #
    #    Mathematically, the update
    #        B[i, j] += sum_{k=i+1}^{M-1} A[k, i] * B[k, j]
    #    over the triangular domain { (i, k) | 0 <= i < k < M } is equivalent to
    #        for k in [0, M):
    #          for all (i, j) with 0 <= i < k:
    #            B[i, j] += A[k, i] * B[k, j]
    #
    #    Inside each (I, J) tile, this can be realized by interchanging
    #    the roles of i and k in the reduction:
    #      - For fixed k, B[k, j] is loaded once and kept in a register.
    #      - The row A[k, *] for this k is streamed once.
    #      - All updates B[i < k, j] that depend on this (k, j) pair are
    #        performed before moving to the next k.
    #
    #    This preserves the original result (up to floating-point
    #    associativity) while greatly increasing reuse of A[k, *] and B[k, j].
    interchange(i, k)

    # 4. Tile the reduction over k to keep the active rows of A and B in
    #    the upper levels of cache:
    #
    #      for K in tiles of k of size TK:
    #        for k in K:
    #          ... reduction body ...
    #
    #    This limits the live working set of A[k, *] and B[k, j] for each
    #    tile, which is particularly important for large M.
    block(k, K, TK)

    # 5. Vectorize the inner loop over k inside the triangular update.
    #
    #    Since k is purely a reduction index and the dependence on k is
    #    only through a sum, the iterations over k can be executed in
    #    SIMD fashion:
    #      - The implementation performs a strip-mined reduction over
    #        chunks of VEC_K consecutive k values.
    #      - This is safe because the only k-carried dependence is the
    #        associative accumulation into B[i, j].
    vectorize(k, VEC_K)

    # 6. Parallelize across column tiles J.
    #
    #    Different columns j of B are completely independent:
    #      - A[k, i] does not depend on j.
    #      - For fixed j, all B[*, j] read/write operations are confined
    #        to that column; no B[*, j1] access affects B[*, j2] for j1 != j2.
    #
    #    Therefore, each J-tile (set of columns) can be processed in a
    #    separate thread without synchronization, both in the update and
    #    in the scale phase:
    #      - Good load balance for large N.
    #      - No additional storage is required (no extra copy of B).
    parallelize(J)

    # 7. Apply the same (i, j) tiling and parallelization to the 'scale'
    #    phase as to 'update'. The scaling loop has no reductions and is
    #    embarrassingly parallel; its primary bottleneck is memory
    #    bandwidth, so sharing the same J-tiled, column-parallel schedule
    #    maximizes reuse of B in caches.
```

```text
    # A is logically a unit lower-triangular MxM matrix.
    # Initialization:
    #   for i in [0,M), k in [0,i):   A[i,k] = ((i + k) % M) / M
    #   for i in [0,M):               A[i,i] = 1
    #   for i in [0,M), k in (i,M):   A[i,k] is unused (left uninitialized)
    #
    # Layout: row-major in (i, k), matching the C/Noarr code's "i then k".
    A[i, k]: in num_t = (i, k) -> i * M + k
        # Only entries A[k, i] with k > i are read in the kernel.

    # B is an MxN dense matrix.
    # Initialization:
    #   for i in [0,M), j in [0,N):
    #       B[i,j] = ((N + (i - j)) % N) / N
    #
    # Layout: row-major in (i, j), matching the original Noarr layout
    # (i outer, j inner), so that j is the fastest-varying index.
    B[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> i * N + j

parameters:
    alpha: num_t            # scalar multiplier from init_array
    M: int                  # number of rows, size of A
    N: int                  # number of columns, size of B

    # Tunable block sizes and SIMD factors (compile-time / config parameters):
    TI: int                 # tile height in i (rows of B), e.g., 32
    TJ: int                 # tile width in j (columns of B), e.g., 64
    TK: int                 # tile depth in k (reduction blocks), e.g., 32
    UJ: int                 # unroll factor for innermost j loop, e.g., 4
    VJ: int                 # vector width (elements) along j, e.g., 4 or 8

computation:
    # Triangular matrix-matrix multiply:
    #   B_out[i,j] = alpha * ( B_in[i,j]
    #                          + sum_{k=i+1..M-1} A[k,i] * B_in[k,j] )
    #
    # Semantics exactly match the given C/Noarr kernel:
    #   - For each (i,j), we start from current B[i,j],
    #   - accumulate contributions A[k,i] * B[k,j] for k > i,
    #   - then scale the final result by alpha.
    #
    # Note: For each fixed column j, there is a sequential dependency along i
    # because B[i,j] depends on all B[k,j] with k > i, but *only* on the
    # original values (no dependence on already updated rows).

    for i in seq(0, M), j in [0, N):
        # High-level scalar expression for the kernel:
        B[i, j] = alpha * (
            B[i, j]
            + sum(k in [i + 1, M), A[k, i] * B[k, j])
        )

optimization:
    # --- 1. Make j the innermost loop inside each i to get a vectorizable kernel ---
    # Original schedule (from the C/Noarr code):
    #   for i in 0..M-1:
    #     for j in 0..N-1:
    #       for k in i+1..M-1:
    #         B[i,j] += A[k,i] * B[k,j]
    #       B[i,j] *= alpha
    #
    # We first express the triangular update and scaling in two explicit phases
    # per row i (purely a re-grouping of operations):
    #   (1) triangular update:  B[i,j] += sum_{k=i+1..M-1} A[k,i] * B[k,j]
    #   (2) scaling:            B[i,j] *= alpha
    #
    # Then, inside the triangular update for a fixed row i, we interchange j and k
    # so that j becomes the innermost loop, which exposes a dense AXPY-like kernel:
    #
    #   for i:
    #     for k = i+1..M-1:
    #       let a_ki = A[k,i]
    #       for j = 0..N-1:
    #         B[i,j] += a_ki * B[k,j]
    #
    # This keeps i sequential and preserves triangular dependencies, but turns
    # the innermost loop into a dense SAXPY over contiguous B[i,*] and B[k,*].

    interchange(j, k)
        # Inside each fixed (i), swap the j and k loops:
        #   before: for j: for k>i: ...
        #   after:  for k>i: for j: ...
        # Algebraically valid because:
        #   - the sum over k is associative/commutative,
        #   - different j are independent.

    # --- 2. Split the computation into "update" + "scale" per row for clarity ---
    # This is just a restructuring, not a semantic change:
    #
    #   UPDATE(i,j):  B[i,j] += sum_{k=i+1..M-1} A[k,i] * B[k,j]
    #   SCALE(i,j):   B[i,j] *= alpha
    #
    # UPDATE uses only the original B[k,j] for k>i (not the updated ones),
    # which is preserved because i stays the outer sequential loop.

    # (Conceptual) label for the triangular update phase
    UPDATE:
        for i in seq(0, M), k in [i + 1, M), j in [0, N):
            B[i, j] += A[k, i] * B[k, j]

    # (Conceptual) label for the scaling phase
    SCALE:
        for i in seq(0, M), j in [0, N):
            B[i, j] *= alpha

    # --- 3. Blocking / tiling for cache locality and better reuse ---

    # 3a) Tile the j dimension (columns of B).
    # This keeps a column block of width TJ in cache during the inner loops.
    # Since j is independent, column tiles can later be parallelized.
    block(j, Jb, TJ)
        # Now we iterate j as:
        #   for Jb in 0..ceil(N/TJ)-1:
        #     for j in tile Jb: ...

    hoist(Jb)
        # Make the column-tile loop outermost within the kernel:
        #   for Jb:
        #     for i:
        #       for k:
        #         for j in tile Jb: ...

    # 3b) Optionally tile the k dimension for better reuse of A[k,i] and B[k,*].
    # For each row i and column-tile Jb, we process k in blocks of size TK.
    # The triangular constraint k > i is handled inside each tile:
    #   k_start = max(i + 1, Kb * TK)
    #   k_end   = min(M, (Kb + 1) * TK)
    block(k, Kb, TK)
    hoist(Kb)
        # Effective nesting (ignoring SCALE phase and triangular guards):
        #   for Jb:                                   # column blocks
        #     for i in 0..M-1:                        # sequential rows
        #       for Kb:                               # k-blocks
        #         for k in block(Kb) with k>i:
        #           a_ki = A[k,i]
        #           for j in tile Jb:
        #             B[i,j] += a_ki * B[k,j]

    # This does not introduce parallelism (i must remain sequential), but
    # helps improve working-set fit.
    block(i, Ib, TI)
    hoist(Ib)
        # i is still visited in increasing order overall, preserving dependencies.

    # --- 4. SIMD and unrolling on the innermost j loop ---

    # With B laid out row-major, the innermost j loop accesses:
    #   B[i,j]   and B[k,j]
    # contiguously in memory. We can vectorize and unroll this loop.

    unroll(j, UJ)

        # loop overhead and improve ILP.

    vectorize(j, VJ)
        # Emit vector instructions over the innermost j-loop (e.g., AVX2/AVX-512),
        # operating on VJ consecutive elements of B[i,*] and B[k,*].

    # --- 5. Parallelization across independent column tiles ---

    # For a fixed column j, B[i,j] depends only on B[k,j] with k > i.
    # Different columns j1 != j2 are completely independent.
    # After tiling j into Jb blocks, each Jb block is still independent.

        # Each worker/thread processes a disjoint tile of columns Jb.
        # Inside a given Jb:

        #   - k-blocking and k loops remain sequential per i,
```

```text
domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)          # row index of A and B
    j: dim in [0, N)          # column index of B
    k: dim in [0, M)          # reduction index over rows of A / B

data:
    # Triangular matrix A: only entries with k >= i are used in the kernel
    # (unit lower-triangular L with L[k, i] = A[k, i] for k >= i, diag = 1.0).
    #
    # We store A in *column-major* layout with respect to (k, i):
    #   - For fixed i, A[k, i] over k is contiguous in memory.
    #   - This matches the kernel access pattern "for fixed i, k = i+1..M-1".
    #
    # Physical address of A[k, i] is: i * M + k
    A[k, i]: in DATA_TYPE = (k, i) -> i * M + k  # column-major in k

    # Rectangular matrix B: M x N, updated in place.
    #
    # We keep B in *row-major* layout (C-like):
    #   - For fixed i, B[i, j] over j is contiguous.
    #   - The optimized schedule will make j the innermost loop to exploit this.
    #
    # Physical address of B[i, j] is: i * N + j
    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE = (i, j) -> i * N + j  # row-major in j

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE          # scalar multiplier
    M: int                    # number of rows of A and B
    N: int                    # number of columns of B

    # Tunable kernel parameters (chosen to respect cache sizes / SIMD width):
    TI: int                   # optional block size in i (e.g., 1–64)
    TJ: int                   # block size in j (e.g., 32–256)
    TK: int                   # block size in k (e.g., 32–256)
    V:  int                   # SIMD vector width used along j (e.g., 4 or 8)
    UK: int                   # unroll factor in k within a tile (e.g., 2–8)

computation:
    # Triangular matrix–matrix multiplication:
    #   B := alpha * L^T * B,
    # where L is the unit lower-triangular matrix stored in A (L[k, i] = A[k, i]).
    #
    # Direct formulation matching the C/Noarr kernel:
    #
    # for (i = 0; i < M; i++)
    #   for (j = 0; j < N; j++) {
    #     Bij = B[i][j];
    #     for (k = i+1; k < M; k++)
    #       Bij += A[k][i] * B[k][j];
    #     B[i][j] = alpha * Bij;
    #   }
    #
    trmm:
        for i in seq(0, M):             # i must be sequential due to B-dependences
            for j in [0, N):
                Bij = B[i, j]
                for k in [i+1, M):
                    Bij = Bij + A[k, i] * B[k, j]
                B[i, j] = alpha * Bij   # final scaling

dependencies:
    # For each column j, updates along i must respect an anti-dependence:
    #   B[i, j] reads B[k, j] for k > i, and B[k, j] is written later
    #   when we process row k for the same column j.
    #
    # Thus, for any fixed j and any i < k, the update at (i, j) must complete
    # before the update at (k, j) can overwrite B[k, j].
    for j in [0, N), i in [0, M), k in [i+1, M):
        trmm(i, j) -> trmm(k, j)

optimization:
    # 1. Use a row-update formulation by interchanging the inner k and j loops.
    #
    #    Starting point (from 'computation'):
    #      for i:
    #        for j:
    #          Bij = B[i, j]
    #          for k = i+1..M-1:
    #              Bij += A[k, i] * B[k, j]
    #          B[i, j] = alpha * Bij
    #
    #    Because there are no dependences across j for fixed i, and the
    #    reduction over k is associative/commutative, we can legally
    #    interchange the j and k loops inside each i to obtain:
    #
    #      for i:
    #        # accumulate contributions from rows k > i into row i
    #        for k = i+1..M-1:
    #            a_ki = A[k, i]              # hoisted out of the j-loop
    #            for j = 0..N-1:
    #                B[i, j] += a_ki * B[k, j]
    #        # final scaling of the whole row i
    #        for j = 0..N-1:
    #            B[i, j] *= alpha
    #
    #    This has two key benefits:
    #      - A[k, i] is loaded once per (i, k) and reused across all N columns.
    #      - B[i, j] and B[k, j] are both accessed as full contiguous rows
    #        when B is stored row-major and j is innermost.
    #
    interchange(j, k)      # inside 'trmm', for fixed i
    hoist(k)               # make 'k' the outer loop over 'j' within each i

    # 2. Block the column (j) and reduction (k) dimensions for cache locality.
    #
    #    After the interchange, the hot part is:
    #      for i:
    #        for k = i+1..M-1:
    #          a_ki = A[k, i]
    #          for j = 0..N-1:
    #            B[i, j] += a_ki * B[k, j]
    #
    #    We tile j and k to operate on cache-sized blocks of B and A:
    #
    #      for i:
    #        for K in [ceil(i+1, TK), ceil(M, TK)):        # k-tiles, respecting k > i
    #          for J in [0, ceil(N, TJ)):                 # j-tiles
    #            for k in [max(i+1, K*TK), min(M, (K+1)*TK)):
    #              a_ki = A[k, i]
    #              for j in [J*TJ, min(N, (J+1)*TJ)):
    #                B[i, j] += a_ki * B[k, j]
    #
    #    This improves temporal reuse of:
    #      - A[k, i] within a k-tile, and
    #      - B[k, j] and B[i, j] within a j-tile.
    #
    block(k, K, TK)        # tile the reduction dimension k into blocks K of size TK
    block(j, J, TJ)        # tile the column dimension j into blocks J of size TJ
    hoist(K)               # process k-tiles outermost (after i) for better A-reuse
    hoist(J)               # process column tiles before inner j (j stays innermost)

    # 3. Optionally block i as well for better interaction with higher cache levels.
    #
    #    i must remain sequential inside each column (due to B-dependencies),
    #    but we can still group rows into i-tiles to improve locality for A's
    #    columns and the corresponding rows of B.
    #
    block(i, I, TI)        # tile rows of B into blocks I of size TI
    hoist(I)               # move I outside of K and J if cache behavior benefits

    # 4. Exploit SIMD by vectorizing the innermost j loop.
    #
    #    Within each (i, K, J) tile, the innermost loop is over j, and B is
    #    row-major, so B[i, j] and B[k, j] are contiguous in memory. We can
    #    therefore vectorize across j:
    #
    #      for i-block I, k-block K, j-block J:
    #        ...
    #        for k in ...:
    #          a_ki = A[k, i]
    #          for j in J-tile step V:
    #            # operate on V consecutive columns at once
    #            B[i, j : j+V-1] += a_ki * B[k, j : j+V-1]
    #
    vectorize(j, V)        # SIMD over j within each tile (V = SIMD width)
    unroll(k, UK)          # unroll k within tiles to increase ILP and reduce overhead

    # 5. Parallelize across independent column tiles.
    #
    #    For a fixed i, different columns j are independent: B[i, j] and B[i, j']
    #    do not depend on each other, and for each j the i-ordering is enforced
    #    by the sequential outer loop. Thus, after tiling over j, we can safely
    #    parallelize over J:
    #
    #      for i in seq(0, M):
    #        parallel for J:
    #          for K:
    #            ...  # row-update TRMM on tile (i, J, K)
    #
    #    This gives thread-level parallelism over column blocks while preserving
    #    the required ordering in i for each column.
    #
    parallelize(J)         # each column tile J can be processed in parallel
```

domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)          # rows of A and B
    j: dim in [0, N)          # columns of B
    k: dim in [0, M)          # reduction index over rows of A/B

data:
    # A is M×M, conceptually indexed as A[i,k]; only entries with k >= i are initialized,
    # and the kernel uses A[k,i] for k > i.  We choose a column‑major layout so that
    # scanning A[k,i] over k (with fixed i) is contiguous in memory.
    A[i, k]: in num_t = (i, k) -> k * M + i
        # column-major: i is the fastest‑varying index

    # B is M×N, indexed as B[i,j].  The kernel repeatedly scans B[k,j] over k (fixed j),
    # and updates B[i,j] once.  We therefore also store B column-major to make both
    # B[k,j] scans and column updates B[i,j] contiguous in i.
    B[i, j]: inout num_t = (i, j) -> j * M + i
        # column-major: i is the fastest‑varying index

parameters:
    alpha: num_t              # scalar multiplier

    # Tuning parameters for blocking and SIMD; chosen empirically for the target CPU/cache.
    TI: int                   # tile size for i (rows)
    TK: int                   # tile size for k (reduction dimension)
    VEC_K: int                # SIMD width used when vectorizing the k-loop

computation:
    # Triangular matrix–matrix multiply (PolyBench TRMM variant).
    #
    # Original kernel:
    #   for (i = 0; i < M; i++)
    #     for (j = 0; j < N; j++) {
    #       for (k = i+1; k < M; k++)
    #         B[i][j] += A[k][i] * B[k][j];
    #       B[i][j] = alpha * B[i][j];
    #     }
    #
    # Semantically:
    #   B[i,j] ← α * ( B[i,j] + Σ_{k=i+1}^{M-1} A[k,i] * B[k,j] )
    #
    # Note: the dependence on B[k,j] means that, for fixed j, all rows must be processed
    # in increasing i so that B[k,j] is still the *original* value when used by row i.
    for i in seq([0, M)):
        for j in [0, N):
            update_B:
                B[i, j] = alpha * (
                    B[i, j]
                    + sum(k in [i + 1, M), A[k, i] * B[k, j])
                )

dependencies:
    # For each column j, row i must be computed before any row k > i, so that
    # B[k,j] is not overwritten before it is read by update_B(i,j).
    for j in [0, N), 0 <= i1 < i2 < M:
        update_B(i1, j) -> update_B(i2, j)

optimization:
    # 1) Loop interchange to improve locality and expose column-wise parallelism.
    #    New order: j outermost, i (sequential) inside, then the k-reduction.
    #    This preserves the i-order per column j required by the dependency above.
    interchange(i, j)

    # 2) Parallelize across columns: columns j are independent given the i-order constraint.
    #    Each parallel worker processes a subset of columns j, with full sequential i
    #    and k loops inside.
    parallelize(j)

    # 3) Block the dependent row dimension i and the reduction dimension k to improve
    #    cache reuse for A and B and reduce working-set size of each inner kernel.
    #
    #    - i is blocked into tiles I of size TI; within each tile, i still runs in
    #      strictly increasing order to respect dependencies.
    #    - k is blocked into tiles K of size TK; within each tile, we will
    #      vectorize kk (the local k) and reuse B[k,j] and A[k,i] from caches.
    block(i, I, TI)           # i = I * TI + ii
    block(k, K, TK)           # k = K * TK + kk

    # Guarding the triangular condition within tiles:
    #   Inside each (I,K) tile, we only execute iterations where kk > i,
    #   i.e., k = K*TK + kk satisfies k > i.  This is equivalent to the
    #   original lower bound k ∈ [i+1, M) and keeps correctness.
    #   (# implemented as an inner if (k > i) around the per-(i,k) work.)

    # 4) Hoist the K-loop outside of the ii-loop so that, within a column j and
    #    an i-tile I, rows of B[k,j] for k in the current K-tile are reused
    #    across many i within the tile.
    hoist(K)

    # 5) Vectorize and unroll along the innermost kk (local k) loop.
    #    With the chosen layouts:
    #      - A[k,i] is contiguous in k for fixed i (column-major A),
    #      - B[k,j] is contiguous in k for fixed j (column-major B),
    #    so the kk loop has unit-stride loads from both A and B, ideal for SIMD.
    vectorize(k, VEC_K)
    unroll(k, VEC_K)

    # 6) Scalar hoisting of A[k,i] within each (i,k) pair to reduce memory traffic:
    #
    #    After the above transformations, the inner structure (within a fixed
    #    column j, tile I, and K-block) is:
    #
    #      for ii in tile I (sequential i):
    #        for kk in tile K with k = K*TK + kk and k > i:
    #          a_ki = A[k, i]                  # load once per (i,k)
    #          for this column j:
    #              B[i, j] += a_ki * B[k, j]

    #    (i,k), keeping it in a register while updating all relevant B[i,j] in

```text
# Optimized model for TRMM kernel (right-side, unit lower-triangular)

domain:
    i: dim in [0, M)        # row index of A and B
    j: dim in [0, N)        # column index of B
    k: dim in [0, M)        # reduction index over rows > i

data:
    # A is conceptually an M×M (unit) lower-triangular matrix.
    # The kernel only ever uses entries with k > i (strictly below the diagonal
    # in the original A[k, i] view).
    #
    # We store the transpose of the original A to get unit-stride access along k:
    #   A_model[i, k]  ≙  A_original[k, i]
    # and use a row-major layout in k.
    #
    # Only the region k > i is actually used; other entries may be left
    # uninitialized, matching the original code.
    A[i, k]: in DATA_TYPE =
        (i, k) -> i * M + k        # row-major: k is fastest-varying

    # B is an M×N matrix, updated in-place.
    #
    # To make accesses B[i, j] and B[k, j] for varying i or k unit-stride,
    # we store B in *column-major* layout: i is fastest-varying, j is outer.
    B[i, j]: inout DATA_TYPE =
        (i, j) -> j * M + i        # column-major: i is fastest-varying

parameters:
    alpha: DATA_TYPE               # scalar multiplication factor

    # Tuning parameters (compile-time or run-time constants):
    TI: int                        # tile size for i (rows)
    TJ: int                        # tile size for j (columns)
    TK: int                        # tile size for k (reduction)
    UK: int                        # unroll factor for k
    VK: int                        # vectorization width over k

computation:
    # Mathematical semantics (using the transposed storage of A):
    #
    # For each (i, j):
    #   B[i, j] ← alpha * ( B[i, j] + Σ_{k = i+1}^{M-1} A[i, k] * B[k, j] )
    #
    # This is equivalent to the original kernel where A[k, i] is used, because
    #   A[i, k] here = A_original[k, i] there.
    #
    update:
        for i in [0, M), j in [0, N):
            Bij = B[i, j]  # register-local accumulator (no extra memory array)
            Bij = Bij + sum(k in [i+1, M), A[i, k] * B[k, j])
            B[i, j] = alpha * Bij

dependencies:
    # B is updated in-place. For correctness, when computing B[i, j] we must
    # read B[k, j] (for k > i) *before* those entries are overwritten.
    #
    # Therefore, for each fixed column j, all row updates must respect:
    #   update(i, j) happens before update(k, j) for all k > i.
    #
    # This exactly matches the partial order of the original nested loops
    # (rows processed in increasing i).
    for j in [0, N), i in [0, M), k in [i+1, M):
        update(i, j) -> update(k, j)

optimization:
    # -------------------------
    # Data-layout optimizations
    # -------------------------
    # 1) Transpose A for better k-access locality:
    #    - Original code uses A_original[k, i] inside the k-loop.
    #    - We instead pre-store A as A[i, k] = A_original[k, i] in row-major
    #      layout so that, for fixed i, increasing k traverses contiguous memory.
    #
    # 2) Store B in column-major layout:
    #    - For fixed column j, accesses B[i, j] (for varying i) and B[k, j]
    #      (for varying k) are both unit-stride along the i dimension.
    #    - This simultaneously optimizes:
    #        * the final write B[i, j] for each (i, j),
    #        * the reads of B[k, j] along k in the inner reduction.

    # -------------------------
    # Loop-structure optimizations
    # -------------------------
    # Baseline semantics use the (i, j) space with the above dependencies.
    # We keep the dependence "increasing i for each fixed j", but change the
    # schedule to exploit the new layouts.

    # 3) Interchange the logical loop order to make j the outermost traversed
    #    dimension and i the next:
    #    - This preserves dependencies because different columns j are
    #      independent, and for each j we still process rows in increasing i.
    interchange(i, j)
    hoist(j)    # ensure j is outermost loop

    # 4) Block (tile) all three dimensions:
    #    - TJ: tile columns to improve reuse of A- and B-rows in cache.
    #    - TI: tile rows so that per-column work over rows fits better in cache.
    #    - TK: tile the k-reduction so both A[i, k] and B[k, j] tiles stay
    #          in L1/L2 cache while accumulating partial sums.
    #

    #        tiles (I is iterated in order, and i inside I is increasing).
    block(j, J, TJ)   # J: tile index over columns
    block(i, I, TI)   # I: tile index over rows
    block(k, K, TK)   # K: tile index over reduction dimension

    hoist(J)          # iterate column tiles outermost
    hoist(I)          # then row tiles, preserving global i order inside each J

    # -------------------------
    # Inner-kernel optimizations
    # -------------------------
    # 5) For each fixed (i, j) inside a tile, the sum over K is a dot product
    #    of:
    #       A[i, k]   for k ∈ [i+1, M)
    #       B[k, j]   for k ∈ [i+1, M)

    #    We therefore:

    unroll(K, UK)      # small unroll factor (e.g., 4–8) tuned empirically

    # -------------------------
    # Parallelization strategy
    # -------------------------
    # 6) Parallelize over column tiles:
    #    - Different columns j (and hence J-tiles) are independent in terms
    #      of data dependencies on B, since dependencies couple only rows i
    #      within a single column j.
    #    - We therefore parallelize the outermost J-loop.
    #    - Inside each column tile J:
    #        * I and i are kept sequential to respect update(i, j) -> update(k, j)
    #          for k > i.
    parallelize(J)

    # Scalar & memory optimizations
    # -------------------------
    # 7) Use a register-local accumulator Bij for each (i, j):
    #    - Load B[i, j] once into Bij, accumulate all A[i, k] * B[k, j]
```
